title: throughput-benchmarking-harness-and-methodology-notes
content:
Goal:
Provide a repeatable, low-noise methodology and harness for throughput benchmarking of the serving runtime. This doc captures load generator config choices, warmup considerations, repeatability checks, instrumentation points, and a basic runbook for running acceptance/regression throughput tests.

Scope and assumptions:
- Focus: end-to-end throughput (tokens/sec) for text-generation and chat-style workloads on the serving runtime.
- Not in scope: quality/eval of outputs, training throughput, or multi-tenant contention modeling (we do basic single-tenant throughput here).
- Hardware and hosting: results must always be annotated with exact instance type, GPU model, driver/CUDA/cuDNN versions, and container base image.

Principles:
- Minimize noise: isolate network and background load, fix clock/time sync, pin CPU governors to performance where applicable.
- Repeatability: deterministic seeds for synthetic load, fixed distribution of sequence lengths, fixed prompt templates.
- Realism: support both synthetic steady-state traces and replaying sampled production traces. Document which was used.
- Clear measurement windows: separate warmup from measurement, discard initial unstable period.

Load generator (loadgen) config recommendations:
- Modes supported: single-request throughput (concurrency=1 with multiple in-flight requests), concurrency mode (N concurrent clients), and batched-mode (driver issues requests that trigger server batching).
- Key parameters:
  - concurrency_clients: number of concurrent client threads/processes.
  - requests_per_client: total requests each client sends (use large enough to reach steady-state, e.g., 2000+).
  - target_qps: optional throttle to control offered load when testing saturation curves.
  - batch_size_hint: preferred inference batch size per request (for models that take batched inputs).
  - seq_length_distribution: explicit distribution vector (e.g., 60% 128 tokens, 30% 256 tokens, 10% 512 tokens) or use exact sequences sampled from production.
  - prompt_variation_count: number of distinct prompt templates to avoid perfect caching artifacts.
- RNG/seeding: provide seed for request generator and shuffle so runs with same seed are repeatable.
- Warmup_count: number of warmup requests to prime caches (see Warmup below).

Warmup and KV-cache priming:
- Warmup is required because the runtime and model kernels optimize over the first N requests (libcudnn/cublas black-box warmups, JIT/kernels compile paths, internal caches).
- Two-layer warmup:
  1) cold-start warmup: a short sequence to ensure all model weights and device memory allocations occur (e.g., 2-5 requests with max sequence length).
  2) steady-state warmup: run enough requests to fill KV caches and stabilize batching behavior (recommendation: 300-1000 requests depending on batch cadence and model).
- When measuring cached vs non-cached performance, explicitly isolate runs ("cold" runs with cache flush between runs using runtime flag or server restart; "warm" runs without flush).
- Document whether cache priming uses identical prompts (more aggressive) or a set of distinct prompts (more realistic).

Measurement windows and statistics:
- Use a three-phase run: initial cold-start (optional), warmup (discarded), measurement window (collect metrics), cooldown (optional).
- Measurement window length: prefer >= 5 minutes for stable percentiles on variable workloads; for microbenchmarks a minimum of 60s with large request counts is acceptable.
- Metrics to record (per-run):
  - aggregate_tokens_per_sec (server-side and client-side)
  - request_count, success_count, error_count
  - latency p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 (look at p99.9 for tail behavior)
  - batching stats: average batch size, batch size distribution, batch latency histogram
  - GPU utilization (%), GPU memory usage (MiB), SM active cycles, power draw (if available)
  - CPU utilization (per core), host memory, network transmit/receive rates
  - kernel compile counts, JIT occurrences, library fallback events (if audit logs available)
  - KV cache hit rate (if exposed)
- For throughput curves: sweep offered load (clients/QPS) and measure sustainable tokens/sec and latency percentiles. Identify knee point where latency degrades non-linearly.

Outlier handling and statistical rigor:
- Remove obvious external noise windows (e.g., background cron jobs). Keep a changelog of environment processes.
- For each configuration run at least 3 independent runs (separate process restarts or container restarts) and report median and interquartile ranges.
- Use bootstrap sampling for percentiles to produce confidence intervals for p95/p99 where possible.
- Avoid reporting single-run numbers unless variability is very low and annotated.

Profiling & bottleneck identification instrumentation:
- Lightweight metrics (always-on during throughput runs): server-side tokens/sec, request latency histograms, batch statistics, queue lengths, scheduler wait times.
- Deep profiling (run separately, not on saturated production sized runs):
  - GPU profiling: nvprof/nsys/nsight with a short representative trace to capture kernel timelines and identify dominant kernels.
  - CPU sampling: perf/top to find threads blocked/waiting or spinning.
  - Tracing: collect end-to-end traces (OpenTelemetry/Jaeger) to correlate request lifecycle with batching and queue times.
  - Memory/alloc traces: track peak device memory, allocation churn, and fragmentation.
- Common bottleneck signals: low GPU utilization + high queuing on host -> CPU or batching overhead; high GPU utilization but latency tail increases -> model kernels hitting saturated SMs or memory bandwidth; high allocator churn -> fragmentation or small-buffer allocations.

Reproducibility checklist (run before publishing a benchmark):
- Hardware metadata: instance SKU, GPU model, driver versions, firmware.
- Software metadata: serving runtime SHA, container image tag, model artifact sha, python package versions.
- Loadgen metadata: seed, prompt sets, seq length distribution, concurrency settings.
- Environment: CPU governor, NUMA bindings, cgroups/limits, background processes.
- Exact command-lines / k8s manifest or docker run args.
- Raw logs and processed metrics attached as artifacts.

Runbook (example):
1) Provision a clean test VM/pod with agreed base image and GPU.
2) Pull container: docker run --rm --gpus all --shm-size=1g -e CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 redwood/serving:sha-XXXX
3) Start server with config: --max-batch-delay-ms=5 --batching=true --kv-cache-size=unbounded --metrics-exporter=prometheus
4) Wait 30s, run cold-start warmup: loadgen --clients=8 --requests-per-client=10 --seq-dist-file=seqs.json --seed=42
5) Run steady-state warmup: loadgen --clients=64 --requests-per-client=500 --seed=42 (discard results)
6) Run measurement: loadgen --clients=64 --requests-per-client=2000 --measure-duration=300 --seed=42 --out=runA.json
7) Collect metrics and profiles: curl metrics endpoint, collect nsys trace for 30s sample, save docker stats, and copy logs.
8) Tear down container, wait 30s, repeat steps 2-7 for 3 runs; change seed or concurrency for curve points.

Artifacts & storage:
- Store run artifacts under a consistent s3 path: s3://redwood-benchmarks/serving-runtime/<date>/<model>/<runtime-sha>/<run-id>/ with raw logs, metrics.json, loadgen output, profiler traces, and a results-summary.json.
- Snapshot any relevant k8s manifests or terraform used for infra creation.

Common pitfalls and notes:
- Small prompt/template sets can artificially inflate batch sizes via identical inputs -> use prompt_variation_count >= 100 for production-like patterns.
- Limitations of synthetic inputs: they may not exercise tokenizer edge-cases which change tokenization length distributions; when in doubt replay sampled production traces.
- Observe and annotate any model-quantization fallbacks or kernel incompatibilities that cause performance cliffs.
- When benchmarking multi-GPU shard/parallel inference, ensure topology (NVLink) and model parallel settings are clearly specified.

Next steps / open questions:
- Standardize a "golden" set of trace workloads (small, medium, large) derived from anonymized production samples.
- Automate the artifact upload + summary generation into a single CI job that runs nightly on dedicated hardware and publishes results to a dashboard.
- Explore statistical tooling to automatically flag regressions using change point detection on p95/p99.

Appendix: example loadgen commands (placeholder)
- loadgen --mode=concurrency --clients=64 --requests-per-client=2000 --seq-dist=seq-dist.json --prompt-src=prompts-1k.json --seed=2024 --out=out.json
- loadgen --mode=throttle --target-qps=20000 --batch-hint=8 --measure-duration=300 --seed=2024

Notes to reviewers:
- Please sanity-check the warmup counts for large models (>30B) — I suspect we need longer steady-state warmup.
- We should align on default measurement window (5 minutes?) and whether to include power draw as a required metric.
- Add any existing prod-trace anonymization guidance if we standardize trace replay.
